newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC chief to give telecom merger speech.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC chief to give telecom merger speech.

text.p: In what is billed as a major speech on merger policy on Thursday, the top U.S. phone regulator is expected to raise more warning flags about AT&T Corp's proposed marriage with SBC Communications Inc .

Outgoing Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt already has been raising questions about such a deal, which, if completed, would create a giant company with a stock market value of $110 billion.
It would be the largest corporate merger in history, although neither company has commented on whether they are holding merger talks.

"I don't think anybody should be too surprised if he says cautionary things about that," said an attorney, who requested anonymity. The FCC has billed the speech as a "major" address. Agency officials declined to comment on the content.
Hundt last week said a mega-merger of AT&T and regional Baby Bell SBC remains "unthinkable" in most antitrust experts' views.

And in a clear reference to AT&T and SBC, Hundt urged regulators "to take an extremely cautious and wary approach" toward proposed mergers involving markets in which previous laws barred the entry of "potentially formidable competitors."

Up until last year's big communciations law, SBC and other Bells were barred from the U.S. long-distance business, while carriers like AT&T effectively were shut out of the local phone market. But the new law set forth a mechanism for doing away with legal barriers that have kept the Bells out of the long-distance business since the break-up of the old Ma Bell phone monopoly in 1984.
The new law also was intended to break open local phone monpolies controlled by the Bells.

AT&T, the number one long-distance company, serves more than 80 million residential customers and 10 million businesses. SBC dominates local phone service in a seven-state area stretching from Texas to California.

"The government knows competition is going to come to the big cities first. And since SBC controls some of the largest metropolitan areas, AT&T in its rumored merger with SBC wouldn't be competing in most of those markets," said analyst Scott Cleland of Legg Mason Precursor Group, the research arm of the Baltimore-based brokerage firm.
Among the big cities already on SBC's turf: Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, Houston, Dallas and San Diego.
In his speech last week, Hundt -- a former antitrust lawyer -- said the government needs to develop "clear and predictable" merger guidelines.
Otherwise, "it will send a message of tolerance to those firms that wish to test the limits of merger policy in newly opened or changing markets," he said.
"It would be better if firms that had little or no chance of persuading government to approve their proposed mergers could be certain of this likelihood," Hundt added.
"Then they might spend less time together in their boardrooms discussing cooperation and more time apart in their separate warrooms discussing competition."
